abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: Glioblastoma (GBM) remains uniformly lethal due to diffuse invasion, extensive molecular heterogeneity, and a profoundly immunosuppressive microenvironment. Nucleic-acid therapeutics—including antisense oligonucleotides, RNA interference, messenger RNA, and CRISPR-based genome editing—offer programmable control over oncogenic drivers and immune pathways, yet their clinical translation is hindered by rapid nuclease degradation, systemic clearance, restricted blood–brain-barrier transport, inefficient cellular uptake, and endosomal entrapment. Recent progress in nanotechnology has enabled the rational design of nanoparticle platforms that overcome these multilayered biological obstacles. This review summarizes advances (2022–2025) in lipid and biomimetic nanocarriers engineered to enhance nucleic-acid delivery for GBM therapy. For instance, ionizable lipid nanoparticles with pH-responsive chemistry and optimized head-group design achieve efficient cytosolic release with improved biocompatibility, while biomimetic systems, such as cell-membrane-, lipoprotein-, virus-, DNA-, and exosome-mimicking platforms, leverage natural transport and recognition pathways for tumor-specific targeting and immune evasion. Finally, we discuss translational considerations, including GMP-compatible manufacturing, batch consistency, long-term safety and immunogenicity, and advanced model selection, and outline future opportunities in high-throughput lipid discovery, AI-assisted ligand design, hydrogel-mediated spatiotemporal release, and patient-tailored nanotherapies. Collectively, these emerging nanocarriers offer a convergent strategy to navigate physiological barriers and advance precision nucleic-acid therapeutics against glioblastoma.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Glioblastoma (GBM) is the most common and lethal primary malignant brain tumor with an incidence of approximately 3–4 cases per 100,000 individuals [1–3]. Despite aggressive multimodality treatment, prognosis is poor since median survival is only around 15 months and five-year survival is less than 10% [4, 5]. The standard of care is maximal safe resection, followed by concurrent radiation and temozolomide (TMZ), followed by adjuvant TMZ therapy [6, 7]. While this leads to a modest prolongation of survival, the effectiveness of this approach is limited by many factors. Notably, radiation and chemotherapy are inherently non-specific and damage healthy neuronal tissue and impair cognition [8]. In addition, development of resistance to TMZ is frequent, leading to tumor relapse after treatment. Moreover, tumor heterogeneity, both genetic and cellular, drives adaptive resistance, therapeutic and immune escape [9–11]. These limitations highlight the urgent need for alternative and more effective therapeutic strategies to overcome immune evasion and improve clinical outcomes in GBM.

Nucleic acid–based therapeutics have emerged as a transformative approach for GBM. These strategies—including antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs), RNA interference (RNAi), messenger RNA (mRNA) therapeutics, and CRISPR-based genome editing—enable direct manipulation of the molecular circuitry that drives tumor initiation and progression [12]. Unlike traditional therapeutics, these nucleic-acid based drug therapeutics target the molecular mediators of the disease and can target any gene including those which are considered undruggable using traditional drug therapy. Once the target sequence is known, they are readily designed, and provide for simple, economical synthesis and development [13]. Specifically, ASOs hybridize to target mRNA, generating degradation of the hybridized mRNA by RNase H-mediated cleavage. RNAi, including small interfering RNA (siRNA) and microRNA (miRNA) silences gene expression post transcriptionally. SiRNAs lead the RNA-induced silencing complex (RISC) to degrade complementary mRNA targets, while miRNA-based interventions lead to modulation of entire networks of gene expression, providing system-based approaches to address the large heterogeneity of the disease process. mRNA based therapies introduce synthetic transcripts that can be translated into tumor suppressive or immunostimulatory proteins, leading to inherent reprogramming of tumor cells or the tumor microenvironment in situ. CRISPR–Cas9 genome editing enables precise and potentially durable correction of oncogenic mutations, deletion of Deoxyribonucleic Acid (DNA) repair genes that lead to chemoresistance, or disruption of stemness-regulatory genes that maintain tumor recurrence [14]. Importantly, in the case of cancer immunotherapy, RNAi or CRISPR may be used to silence molecules mediating immune checkpoints that lead to T-cell exhaustion. On the other hand, mRNA constructs could provide cytokines or tumor antigens that favor dendritic cell activation that leads to expansion of cytotoxic T-cells [15]. Thus, nucleic acid therapeutics represent a new and promising approach in achieving effective therapy for patients with GBM.

Despite the expectation that nucleic acid therapeutics hold for the treatment of tumors, they are limited by a complex set of biologic barriers that preclude effective delivery to glioblastoma. The first major barrier consists of systemic instability and rapid clearance (Fig. 1A). Once administered to the systemic circulation, naked nucleic acids are subject to extensive enzymatic degradation by circulating nucleases, which results in extremely short half-life in circulation. The anionic charge associated with the nucleic acids serves to enhance rapid renal clearance and the opsonization by serum proteins, which lead to sequestration by the mononuclear phagocyte system within the liver and spleen [16, 17]. Thus, only a small fraction of the nucleic acid could endure long enough in the circulation to reach the site of entry into the central nervous system. In the small fraction that survives in the systemic circulation, the next barrier to be overcome is that devoted to the blood-brain barrier (BBB), or the heterogeneous blood-tumor barrier (BTB) (Fig. 1B-C). The BBB is a highly selective surface consisting of tightly joined endothelial cells, active transporters for efflux, and extensive enzymatic activity which inhibits entry into the brain of macromolecules. Hence, it is difficult for free nucleic acid to passively diffuse across these barriers [18, 19]. If by chance the free nucleic acid penetrates the BBB or BTB, another major barrier is the entry of the nucleic acid (Fig. 1C). The anionic phospholipid bilayer of the cell membrane in the brain serves likewise to electrostatically repel the negatively charged nucleic acid backbone. Thus, free nucleic acids are poorly internalized [20]. For those nucleic acids after cell internalization, nucleic acids are almost trafficked into the endosomal–lysosomal pathway. Without engineered properties, they are trapped in endosomes, which acidify and fuse with enzyme-filled lysosomes, leading to rapid enzymatic degradation (Fig. 1D) [21]. Additionally, for siRNA and mRNA to participate in gene silencing and protein expression, they must engage with the RNA interference complex or ribosomes, respectively [22]. With respect to plasmid DNA, it must cross the nuclear envelope, a primary barrier, to allow transcription (Fig. 1E) [23]. These barriers indicate the need for advanced delivery systems capable of protecting nucleic acids, targeting them precisely to tumor cells, and releasing them in a controlled manner to overcome GBM’s multifaceted barriers.

B The blood–brain barrier (BBB) and heterogeneous blood–tumor barrier (BTB) restrict entry into brain tumors. C The anionic plasma membrane of glioblastoma cells repels negatively charged nucleic acids, reducing cellular uptake. D Internalized nucleic acids are trapped in endosomes and degraded in lysosomes. E Functional activity requires cytosolic release for siRNA/mRNA or nuclear entry for plasmid DNA, processes that free nucleic acids lack

sec.p: Nanoparticles have emerged as one of the most promising technological solutions to overcome the complex barriers that limit free nucleic acid delivery to glioblastoma. With careful design, such carriers can be built that will protect nucleic acid cargo while prolonging systemic circulation, getting through the blood-brain barrier and blood-tumor barrier, promoting tumor selective uptake while facilitating intracellular release of the cargo that will assist in alleviating tumor specific barriers and greatly improve therapeutic utility. Previous reviews largely reported the progress of nanoparticle-mediated delivery of chemotherapeutic drugs for GBM [24, 25]. In contrast, this review summarizes recent advances (2022–2025) in nanoparticle-mediated nucleic-acid delivery for GBM, with a particular focus on lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) and biomimetic nanoplatforms—including cell-membrane coatings, lipoprotein- and virus (bacteriophage)-like architectures, DNA-based nanostructures and engineered exosomes (Fig. 2). We conclude with a forward-looking outlook on the translational potential, emerging challenges, and future directions of this rapidly evolving field.

Representative nanoparticle systems discussed in this review include lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) and biomimetic nanoparticles, including lipoprotein-like, virus (bacteriophage)-like architectures, DNA-based nanoparticles, and engineered exosomes

sec.title: LNPs in glioblastoma therapy
sec.p: LNPs are versatile, self-assembled nanocarriers composed of ionizable and/or cationic lipids, helper lipids, cholesterol and polyethylene glycol-lipids [26]. Depending on the formulation, LNPs can be broadly characterized as solid lipid nanoparticles, cationic liposomes, or ionizable LNPs designed for nucleic acid delivery. LNPs provide superior biocompatibility, scalable manufacturing, and efficient delivery of various payloads. Their modular design enables precise tuning of particle size, charge, and surface chemistry to optimize biodistribution and cellular uptake [27].

sec.title: LNP strategies for BBB penetration and intracellular release
Ligand-mediated targeting strategies for BBB transport and glioblastoma-specific uptake
sec.p: Ligand-mediated targeting represents a central strategy for enabling nanoparticle delivery to glioblastoma by addressing two sequential biological barriers: (i) transport across the blood–BBB, and (ii) selective uptake by tumor cells within the brain parenchyma. Effective targeting strategies therefore require coordinated engagement of receptors expressed on brain endothelial cells to enable transcytosis, followed by interaction with tumor-associated receptors to promote preferential accumulation within glioblastoma tissue.

sec.title: BBB transport targets enabling nanoparticle entry into the brain
sec.p: Receptor-mediated transcytosis (RMT) represents one of the most extensively exploited mechanisms for nanoparticle transport across the BBB. This physiological process enables selective transcellular transport of macromolecules through coordinated receptor binding, vesicular internalization, intracellular trafficking, and abluminal release into the brain interstitium. Following ligand binding, receptor–nanoparticle complexes undergo clathrin- or caveolae-mediated endocytosis and are trafficked through early and sorting endosomes. At this stage, intracellular sorting determines delivery efficiency: nanoparticles may recycle back to the luminal membrane, undergo lysosomal degradation, or undergo productive transcytosis involving vesicular transport to the abluminal membrane and release into the brain parenchyma. Efficient BBB transport therefore requires receptor engagement and intracellular trafficking pathways that favor transcytosis rather than degradation or recycling [28–30].

Among BBB transport pathways, the transferrin receptor (TfR) remains the most extensively validated and widely utilized target for nanoparticle-mediated brain delivery. TfR is highly expressed on brain endothelial cells and mediates physiological iron transport into the central nervous system through clathrin-mediated endocytosis and vesicular transcytosis. Nanoparticles functionalized with transferrin, anti-TfR antibodies, or TfR-binding peptides exploit this pathway to achieve enhanced BBB penetration [31, 32]. However, recent in vivo imaging studies have demonstrated that vascular transport dynamics strongly influence delivery efficiency. TfR-targeted nanoparticles are internalized throughout the brain microvasculature but undergo productive transcytosis primarily at post-capillary venules rather than capillaries or arterioles. Although endothelial uptake occurs across vessel types, transcytosis-mediated brain entry is largely restricted to post-capillary venules, where the presence of a perivascular space provides a permissive anatomical environment facilitating nanoparticle exit from endothelial cells and subsequent distribution into brain tissue. In contrast, capillaries, despite high TfR expression, frequently retain internalized nanoparticles within endothelial cells, limiting effective transport. These findings identify post-capillary venules as a key anatomical gateway for nanoparticle brain entry and highlight vascular segment–specific endothelial architecture as a critical determinant of delivery efficiency [33].

Ligand design parameters and physiological competition further influence TfR-mediated transport [34]. High endogenous transferrin can compete for receptor binding [32], and ligand affinity strongly impacts sorting: very high affinity can increase lysosomal routing, while moderate affinity/monovalent binding can favor transcytosis [35, 36]. Species-specific differences in TfR structure and trafficking represent a major translational challenge [37]. Many TfR-targeting ligands exhibit species-selective binding, and ligands optimized for murine TfR often do not bind human TfR with comparable affinity or trafficking behavior [38]. Human transferrin receptor knock-in mouse models have been developed to address this limitation by replacing the endogenous murine receptor with the human TfR sequence, enabling evaluation of human-specific targeting ligands [39–41]. However, important limitations remain, as other key determinants of BBB transport, including endothelial trafficking machinery, receptor expression density, vascular ultrastructure, and systemic pharmacokinetics remain murine [42]. Non-human primate studies, which more closely reflect human physiology [43, 44], frequently demonstrate lower CNS delivery efficiency and increased peripheral sequestration compared with rodent models [45]. These findings emphasize that successful delivery in rodent models does not necessarily predict human clinical performance and highlight the importance of designing nanoparticle targeting strategies optimized for human receptor biology and transport mechanisms.

Apolipoprotein-based targeting strategies provide physiologically relevant pathways for BBB transport. Apolipoprotein E (ApoE) and ApoE-derived peptides interact with low-density lipoprotein receptor (LDLR) family members and low-density lipoprotein receptor-related protein-1 (LRP1), which mediate endogenous lipoprotein transport across the BBB [46]. Nanoparticles exploiting these pathways demonstrate enhanced brain accumulation and may enable sequential BBB transport and tumor cell uptake. Rabies virus glycoprotein (RVG)-derived peptides represent another important class of BBB-targeting ligands. RVG binds nicotinic acetylcholine receptors expressed on brain endothelial and neuronal cells, facilitating receptor-mediated transcytosis and improved central nervous system delivery [47].

Cell-penetrating peptides, including TAT and penetratin, provide an alternative receptor-independent transport mechanism through adsorptive-mediated transcytosis [48]. These peptides promote electrostatic interactions with negatively charged proteoglycans on endothelial cell surfaces, triggering vesicular internalization and transcellular transport. However, limited specificity and increased uptake by peripheral tissues may reduce delivery selectivity and translational efficiency [49].

sec.title: Glioblastoma-specific targets enabling selective tumor cell uptake
sec.p: Following BBB transport, selective uptake by glioblastoma cells represents a second critical determinant of therapeutic efficacy. Glioblastoma exhibits characteristic overexpression of tumor-associated receptors that can be exploited to enhance tumor-specific nanoparticle internalization.

The epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR), including the tumor-specific mutant EGFRvIII, is amplified or overexpressed in approximately 40–60% of glioblastoma cases. EGFR-targeting ligands—including EGF-derived peptides, anti-EGFR antibodies, and antibody fragments—enable receptor-mediated internalization and enhanced tumor cell uptake. Interleukin-13 receptor α2 (IL13Rα2), which exhibits minimal expression in normal brain tissue but high expression in glioblastoma, represents another highly tumor-selective target. IL-13–derived ligands and IL13Rα2-specific targeting peptides enable selective nanoparticle delivery to tumor cells [50–52].

Glioblastoma stem cell (GSC) populations, which contribute to therapeutic resistance and tumor recurrence, frequently overexpress stem cell markers such as CD133 and CD44 [53–55]. Targeting these receptors enables preferential delivery to tumor-initiating cells and may improve therapeutic durability. Additional tumor-associated receptors, including EphA2, platelet-derived growth factor receptor (PDGFR), folate receptor α, and LAT1, further expand the repertoire of glioblastoma-specific targeting strategies. Folate and hyaluronic acid conjugation targeted folate receptors and CD44 on cancer cells, respectively [53–55].

Integrins αvβ3 and αvβ5 are highly expressed on both glioblastoma cells and tumor vasculature. RGD-functionalized nanoparticles targeting these integrins enhance tumor retention and cellular internalization [56, 57]. However, integrin targeting primarily improves tumor uptake rather than BBB transcytosis, highlighting the importance of combining tumor-targeting ligands with BBB transport ligands to achieve efficient brain delivery.

In addition to improving BBB transport through early formulations of LNPs, there were attempts to improve cytoplasmic delivery of agents. These systems largely employed the same cationic lipids such as DOTAP, DOTMA, DC-Chol, DOSPA, and DMRIE to complex with nucleic acids via electrostatic forces and to promote cellular uptake. However, the high cytotoxicity of these systems invariably resulted in tissue damage and failure to translate into clinical utility [58].

sec.title: Protein corona formation and the balance between targeting and stealth
sec.p: Following systemic administration, LNPs rapidly adsorb plasma proteins, forming a dynamic protein corona that defines their biological identity in vivo [59, 60]. This corona commonly contains albumin, apolipoproteins (e.g., apolipoprotein E, ApoE), complement components, and immunoglobulins. Its composition is governed by nanoparticle surface chemistry, charge, polyethylene glycol (PEG) density, and ligand presentation [59–61].

Protein corona formation directly influences BBB transport and intracellular trafficking. Adsorbed proteins may mask engineered targeting ligands, reducing receptor accessibility and impairing receptor-mediated transcytosis [62]. Conversely, enrichment of ApoE on nanoparticle surfaces can facilitate uptake through low-density lipoprotein receptor (LDLR) or low-density lipoprotein receptor–related protein 1 (LRP1) pathways, enabling endogenous receptor engagement independent of synthetic ligands [63]. Corona composition can further bias intracellular fate, directing nanoparticles toward productive transcytosis or lysosomal degradation depending on surface physicochemical properties.

These considerations highlight the need to balance active targeting with stealth properties that preserve systemic stability. PEGylation reduces nonspecific protein adsorption, complement activation, and macrophage clearance, thereby prolonging circulation [64, 65]. in LNP systems, PEG–lipid composition, PEG-Lipid-DNA interaction and dissociation kinetics critically influence circulation half-life and biodistribution [66, 67]. However, excessive ligand density may disrupt PEG shielding and promote opsonization, while excessive PEG density can sterically hinder receptor binding and reduce uptake efficiency [68]. Recent mRNA-LNP studies further demonstrate that PEG architecture and surface composition modulate protein corona structure and immune recognition, influencing delivery efficiency. Optimal nanoparticle design therefore requires careful tuning and control of ligand density [69], PEG molecular weight, and surface charge and density optimization [70–72], and particle size to balance targeting efficiency, pharmacokinetics, and immune compatibility [73–78].

sec.title: Biological bypass and physical BBB modulation
sec.p: One particularly promising direction involves biological bypass strategies that circumvent the BBB altogether. A representative example is the work by Hu et al. (2022), who developed a non-invasive, biologically driven approach for intranasal administration of a multifunctional, 1,2-dioleoyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphoethanolamine (DOPE)-based core–shell lipoplex encapsulating c-MYC-targeting siRNA. The silence of c-MYC resulted in the interruption of oncogenic transcriptional networks that control the regulation of cell proliferation and metabolic activity, with attendant outcomes of tumor growth suppression and apoptosis. The siRNA was condensed with octa-arginine (R8) peptide and further modified with the penetratin derived peptide, named 89WP, a peptide that has been extensively studied as a brain-homing and membrane displacement peptide that permits nose to brain delivery. The 89WP sequence increased epithelial permeability and resulted in the stimulation of macropinocytosis, while the R8 core and DOPE liposome promoted the destabilization of endosomal membranes and the cytoplasmic delivery of siRNA. The formulation design permits the delivery of siRNA directly to the glioma tissues avoiding vascular barriers. In orthotopic GBM bearing mice, the administered 89WP- core–shell lipoplex (CLS)/R8/siRNA via intranasal route segregated preferentially to the tumor, suppressed c-MYC at the transcript level, and produced a very marked median survival increase without nasal or systemic toxicity [79]. Collectively, this study exemplifies how the use of brain-homing peptides, fusogenic lipid chemistry combined with non-invasive methods of delivery can permit the circumvention of vascular and intracellular barriers, thus establishing a biocompatible platform for effective RNA delivery to brain via the non-invasive route for glioblastoma therapy.

In addition to intranasal delivery, other clinically established bypass routes include intrathecal and intracerebroventricular administration, which deliver therapeutics directly into cerebrospinal fluid and circumvent the BBB entirely. These approaches have demonstrated clinical success in neurological disorders, including ASO therapies such as nusinersen. Direct central nervous system (CNS) administration enables immediate exposure of therapeutic nanoparticles to brain and spinal cord tissues, avoiding systemic clearance and receptor-mediated transport limitations. Although more invasive than systemic delivery, these routes may be particularly advantageous for LNP-mediated nucleic acid delivery when high CNS exposure is required or when BBB transport is inefficient. Furthermore, intrathecal or intracerebroventricular administration may be combined with optimized LNP formulations to improve nanoparticle distribution within the CNS, enhance cellular uptake, and increase therapeutic efficacy for glioblastoma.

Beyond biological bypass strategies, physical modulation of the BBB using focused ultrasound (FUS) in combination with microbubbles (MB) has emerged as a complementary approach to enhance LNP delivery to the brain. This strategy addresses limitations associated with ligand-dependent targeting, including receptor saturation and restricted tissue penetration, by transiently and locally increasing BBB permeability without causing permanent vascular damage. In a recent study, Shumer-Elbaz et al. (2025) optimized low-frequency FUS parameters to induce controlled MB oscillations, enabling safe and reversible BBB opening and facilitating nanoparticle extravasation into both normal brain and tumor tissues (Fig. 3A). Two ionizable lipids, Lipid-14 and SM-102, were evaluated for nucleic acid delivery efficiency. Luciferase mRNA–loaded LNPs formulated with either lipid demonstrated significantly increased bioluminescence expression when combined with MB and FUS compared with LNP administration alone (Fig. 3B–C). In orthotopic GBM models, Cy5-labeled siRNA-LNPs exhibited a 6–7-fold increase in intratumoral fluorescence intensity following combined MB and FUS treatment relative to FUS alone (Fig. 3D–E) [80]. These findings support low-frequency FUS combined with MB-induced cavitation as a non-invasive strategy to enhance RNA–LNP delivery across the BBB and improve intratumoral accumulation.

sec.p: Although FUS combined with microbubbles represents a clinically promising strategy for transient BBB modulation, practical considerations remain. The safety and reproducibility of repeated BBB opening sessions, particularly in patients requiring chronic treatment, must be carefully evaluated. Parameters such as acoustic pressure, microbubble dose, and treatment frequency require standardization to balance delivery efficiency with preservation of vascular integrity. Long-term monitoring of neuroinflammation, vascular remodeling, and cumulative exposure effects will be important for broader clinical implementation.

sec.title: Emerging ligand-mediated receptor transcytosis
sec.p: Although FUS is a physical method of producing a physiological opening of the BBB, the molecular approach has been directed towards the solution of the issues associated with conventional ligand-mediated delivery. Specifically, in recent times, the situation has developed when next generation targeting ligands has been successful and can show more selectivity and.

transport efficiency. Angiopep- 2 which is a targeting peptide derived from the Kunitz domain of aprotinin, has emerged as a candidate because of its stated effectiveness and affinity for LRP1 which is a molecule very abundantly expressed in both glioma cells and BBB endothelial cells [81]. This dual-targeting capability enables a two-stage delivery process: efficient receptor-mediated transcytosis across the BBB followed by selective uptake into tumor cells. Compared with other targeting ligands such as transferrin or lactoferrin, Angiopep-2 exhibits markedly higher affinity and achieves greater brain penetration efficiencies. Tong et al. (2025) made use of these molecular features in the preparation of an optimized ionizable lipid nanoparticle (LNP) formulation, SPLK1/Ang-C2 LNP, using a combination of SM-102 (an ionizable lipid), 1,2-distearoyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphocholine (DSPC), cholesterol, and 1,2-dimyristoyl-rac-glycero-3-methoxypolyethylene glycol-2000 (DMG-PEG 2000), which was further coupled with 1,2-distearoyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphoethanolamine-polyethylene glycol (DSPE-PEG)-Angiopep-2 to facilitate active transport across the BBB and subsequent intracellular delivery. The SM-102 core, facilitated by protonation at low pH, shows a capacity to undergo endosomal membrane fusion and allow for the release of cytoplasmic small interfering RNA (siRNA). While PEGylation limits opsonization and provides a prolonged circulation time allowing for a greater opportunity for the active targeting of low-density lipoprotein receptor-related protein 1 (LRP1) receptors. This formulation achieved one of the highest reported brain-delivery efficiencies for the studied LNPs. When loaded with siRNA targeting polo-like kinase 1 (PLK1), a mitotic regulator frequently overexpressed in GBM, this LNP platform significantly inhibited tumor growth and prolonged median survival in orthotopic GBM models [82]. This study shows that receptor transcytosis was used to address the two barriers associated with GBM therapy, by the application of Angiopep-2 peptide, and can be ameliorated via an SM-102 based, pH sensitive, LNP platform for easy endosomal escape out of cellular compartments. Although the Angiopep-2 peptide was used, a number of novel BBB-associated peptides have been discovered recently and reviewed extensively, but their use for nucleic acid delivery in glioblastoma has not been reported [83].

sec.title: Novel ionizable lipid design and chemistry-driven optimization
sec.p: Chemical optimization of ionizable lipid components has become a powerful means to enhance intracellular delivery. Liu et al. (2022) reported a chemistry-guided strategy for the rational design of ionizable lipids optimized for small interfering RNA (siRNA) delivery and immune modulation in glioblastoma (GBM). Through systematic lipid library screening, the authors fine-tuned amine headgroup structure and apparent pKa values to balance protonation capacity for endosomal escape with biocompatibility. Among the candidates, BAMPA-O16B emerged as the lead lipid, demonstrating efficient endosomal destabilization, robust gene-silencing activity, and low cytotoxicity. A key property of BAMPA-O16B is its pH-responsive behavior, transitioning from a near-neutral state at physiological pH to a positively charged state within the acidic endosomal environment. Protonation under endosomal conditions promotes electrostatic interactions with anionic endosomal phospholipids, leading to membrane destabilization and facilitating cytosolic release of siRNA prior to lysosomal degradation. The authors formulated BAMPA-O16B/siRNA lipoplexes encapsulating siRNAs targeting programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) and CD47, two immune checkpoint regulators that contribute to GBM immune evasion. This dual-delivery strategy simultaneously blocked the “don’t eat me” signal on tumor cells and suppressed immune checkpoint pathways, thereby enhancing macrophage-mediated phagocytic clearance and reactivating cytotoxic T-cell responses within the tumor microenvironment. A systemic delivery of the LNPs in the orthotopic animal brain model of GBM achieved significant knockdown of PD-L1 and CD47, increased intratumoral T-cell infiltration, and inhibited tumor growth [84]. When compared to Lipid-14, a non-biodegradable lipidoid structure, and SM-102 with partial-rate of biodegradability, as previously mentioned, BAMPA-O16B has many additional advantages due to its biocompatibility, through its biodegradability in structures type β-amino-ester based scaffold, enhancing rate of tissue clearance, decreasing tissue accumulation, exhibiting less reactogenicity, and being favorable for repeated dosing, leading to long-term depot for the efficacious delivery of nucleic-acids.

In addition to the BAMPA-O16B system, Cao et al. (2025) reported a chemistry-guided lipid engineering strategy based on the synthesis of SR-57,227–derived ionizable lipids. SR-57,227 is a small molecule capable of crossing the BBB via serotonin 5-hydroxytryptamine receptor 3 (5-HT3)–mediated transport. Following systematic screening, the authors identified S4 as a lead lipid for brain mRNA delivery and developed an optimized LNP formulation termed OS4. To further enhance delivery efficiency, the formulation was modified with the cell-penetrating peptide Tat, generating the OS4T LNP platform. This modification resulted in an approximately 12-fold increase in brain mRNA delivery compared with the unmodified OS4 formulation. Mechanistically, SR-57,227–derived lipids facilitated 5-HT3 receptor–mediated transcytosis, whereas Tat promoted caveolae- and macropinocytosis-dependent uptake, collectively enhancing transendothelial transport. Compared with the clinically approved LNP formulation (Onpattro®), OS4T demonstrated substantially increased mRNA translation in brain tissue. The platform enabled delivery of engineered interleukin-12 (eIL-12) mRNA to multiple brain cell types. In a GBM model, OS4T–eIL-12 treatment suppressed tumor growth and prolonged median survival from 17 to 37 days [85].

sec.title: LNP for reprogramming tumor resistance and immunosuppression
sec.p: Tumor-inherent resistance and the highly immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment constitute major impediments to securing durable long-term therapeutic benefit in GBM. Whereas Sect. ''LNP Strategies for BBB Penetration and Intracellular Release'' focused on the chemistry and delivery strategies that enable (LNPs—particularly ionizable LNPs—to penetrate the BBB, achieve tumor accumulation, and escape the endosome, Sect. ''LNP for Reprogramming Tumor Resistance and Immunosuppression'' focuses on how LNP platforms are now being applied to actively overcome therapy resistance. Specifically, this section highlights emerging LNP-based strategies designed to overcome temozolomide (TMZ) resistance, restore apoptotic competence, and remodel the immunosuppressive microenvironment that drives GBM persistence.

sec.title: LNP for overcoming TMZ resistance and restoring TMZ sensitivity
sec.p: Liu et al. (2022) developed a 2-deoxy-D-glucose–modified lipid–polymer hybrid nanoparticle co-loaded with TMZ and siRNA targeting programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1), designated TMZ/siPD-L1@GLPN/dsb. This platform was designed to integrate chemotherapeutic sensitization with immune checkpoint modulation to address TMZ resistance and immunosuppression in GBM.In orthotopic TMZ-resistant GBM models, the nanoplatform facilitated coordinated delivery of TMZ and siPD-L1. PD-L1 silencing increased the proportion of CD3⁺CD8⁺IFN-γ⁺ cytotoxic T lymphocytes while reducing CD4⁺CD25⁺FoxP3⁺ regulatory T cells, indicating enhanced antitumor immune activity. Concurrently, the formulation restored TMZ sensitivity through downregulation of O⁶-methylguanine-DNA methyltransferase (MGMT), a key mediator of chemoresistance. This combined approach suppressed tumor growth and prolonged survival in orthotopic GBM-bearing rats. Collectively, these findings illustrate how LNP–based co-delivery strategies can simultaneously modulate tumor-intrinsic resistance mechanisms and tumor-associated immune suppression [86].

Recent studies have identified miR-603 and miR-221 as post-transcriptional regulators that suppress MGMT expression, thereby restoring TMZ sensitivity in GBM. Building on this observation, Abate et al. (2025) developed self-assembling ionizable nanoparticles (SANPs) encapsulated miR-603 and miR-221 to address TMZ resistance. In vitro MTT and clonogenic assays demonstrated synergistic effects between miRNA co-delivery and TMZ treatment, resulting in reduced cell viability and clonogenic potential in GBM cells. In orthotopic xenograft mouse models, combined treatment with miRNA-loaded SANPs and TMZ inhibited tumor growth and prolonged survival compared with monotherapy. These findings support SANP-mediated miRNA co-delivery as a strategy to reverse chemoresistance and enhance TMZ efficacy in GBM. This study demonstrates a nanotherapeutic approach wherein SANP-based co-delivery of miRNAs is applied to effectively reverse chemoresistance and potentiate TMZ efficacy in GBM treatment [87].

sec.title: LNP for overcoming apoptosis resistance and remodeling the immunosuppressive microenvironment
sec.p: Beyond strategies aimed solely at overcoming temozolomide (TMZ) resistance, Song et al. (2024) investigated the role of excision repair cross-complementation group 2 (ERCC2) in GBM and developed DOTAP–mPEG–PCL (DMC) nanoparticles for targeted delivery of ERCC2-specific siRNA. ERCC2 expression was significantly elevated in GBM tissues and correlated with poorer patient prognosis. Functional analyses indicated that ERCC2 promotes GBM cell proliferation, migration, and tumor growth. ERCC2 silencing induced G0/G1 cell cycle arrest and suppressed the CDK2/CDK4/CDK6–Cyclin D1/D3 signaling axis. Mechanistic studies further demonstrated a direct interaction between ERCC2 and cyclin-dependent kinase 4 (CDK4), influencing its transcriptional regulation and downstream expression. ERCC2 knockdown also increased cellular sensitivity to tumor necrosis factor–related apoptosis-inducing ligand (TRAIL), a cytokine that selectively induces apoptosis in malignant cells. Combined treatment with DMC–siERCC2 and TRAIL enhanced apoptosis in vitro and reduced tumor growth in xenograft models without detectable systemic toxicity. These findings support ERCC2 as a functional contributor to GBM progression and suggest that nanoparticle-mediated siERCC2 delivery in combination with TRAIL may represent a strategy to overcome TRAIL resistance [88].

Recent studies have progressed beyond targeting intrinsic resistance pathways to actively remodeling the tumor microenvironment. In addition to the ionizable LNP systems co-delivery siRNAs against CD47 and PD-L1developed by the Liu group described in Sect. ''LNP Strategies for BBB Penetration and Intracellular Release'', Yang et al. (2025) reported an LNP-based platform designed to modulate the immunosuppressive glioblastoma (GBM) microenvironment. The authors engineered immunomodulatory lipid nanoparticles (ULNPs) in which ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA) partially substituted for cholesterol. These ULNPs delivered a circular RNA (circRNA) encoding an interleukin-2–Fc fusion protein (IL-2 F). The circRNA construct provided enhanced enzymatic stability and prolonged protein expression relative to linear messenger RNA (mRNA), resulting in approximately 2.9-fold higher intratumoral IL-2 F levels and sustained expression for up to 10 days. The ULNP formulation exhibited dual functionality: the lipid components facilitated cytosolic delivery through endosomal escape, while UDCA promoted autophagic degradation of transforming growth factor-β1 (TGF-β1), a key mediator of regulatory T cell (Treg) differentiation and immunosuppression. To achieve spatial control, ULNPs encapsulating circRNA-IL-2 F were incorporated into an injectable biodegradable hydrogel, enabling localized and sustained release within the tumor resection cavity. This approach increased CD8⁺ T cell expansion and activation while reducing Treg infiltration, resulting in an elevated CD8⁺/Treg ratio exceeding 2.5. In orthotopic GBM models, this combination induced durable tumor regression, with induced great tumor regression remission, and reduced post-surgical recurrence, without evidence of the systemic cytokine elevation or hepatotoxicity commonly associated with interleukin-2 (IL-2) therapy [89].

Collectively, these studies chart the evolution of LNP-based nanotherapy for GBM—from metabolic and DNA-repair reprogramming to integrated chemo-immune synergy, multi-RNA network control, apoptosis restoration, and ultimately, comprehensive immunological remodeling of the glioblastoma microenvironment.

sec.title: LNPs for genome editing to overcome multibarrier constraints
sec.p: With recent advances in barrier-adaptive tumor reprogramming and delivery, research efforts are translating advances in genome intervention to the technology of the ionizable LNPs as a means of achieving CRISPR genome editing with the accuracy this offers, as a therapeutic modality in GBM nanomedicine. Genome editing represents an emerging therapeutic strategy with potential for durable genetic modulation in GBM. Unlike with the transient delivery of RNA interference systems or mRNA systems inducing transcript replacements, CRISPR systems have the capacity to achieve permanent genetic reprogramming, with the accompanying advantages to be gained from long-term therapeutic efficacy [89]. Accordingly, engineered LNPs have been produced with genome-editing capabilities that address the complex, multibarrier microenvironmental landscape of GBM while preserving the biocompatibility of multiple cancer therapies.

Among recent developments, Zhang et al. (2025) reported miRTEN, a lipid nanoparticle (LNP) platform designed for co-delivery of CRISPR–Cas9 components targeting microRNA-10b (miR-10b), a key regulator of glioblastoma (GBM) pathogenesis. The system encapsulated Cas9 mRNA and a single-guide RNA (sgRNA) directed against miR-10b. The formulation incorporated the ionizable lipid LP-01, selected for neuronal delivery efficiency and biodegradability, enabling pH-dependent endosomal escape while reducing hepatic accumulation relative to commonly used lipids such as SM-102. Following intracerebroventricular administration, the LNPs achieved tumor-enriched distribution and mediated gene-editing efficiencies of approximately 85% in cultured GSCs and 30–75% in orthotopic tumor tissues in vivo. It was also found that miR-10b disruption suppressed GSC proliferation, invasion, and self-renewal. In addition to inducing tumor cell apoptosis, treatment was associated with modulation of the tumor microenvironment, including increased CD8⁺ T cell infiltration and reduced immunosuppressive signaling. These effects correlated tumor regression and prolonged survival in murine GBM models. Combination treatment with TMZ further enhanced therapeutic response and improved survival in resistant tumors [90]. Similarly, Zhao et al. (2024) introduced a polymer-locking fusogenic liposome, Plofsome, that achieved ROS-triggered BBB penetration and cytoplasmic delivery of siRNA and CRISPR–Cas9 ribonucleoprotein complexes targeting midkine (MDK), a key regulator of TMZ resistance in GBM. The system utilized a 4-arm polyethylene glycol-ortho-diphenol (4-arm PEG-oDP) polymer, which acted as a ‘lock’ by anchoring to the brain-targeted fusogenic liposome via ROS-cleavable boronate linkers. This design maintained the Plofsomes in a non-fusogenic state during systemic circulation and transcytosis across the BBB, preventing premature fusion and off-target release. Upon entering the oxidative tumor microenvironment, elevated ROS levels cleaved the boronate bonds, detaching the PEG-oDP layer and restoring fusogenicity. The unlocked Plofsomes then fused directly with GBM cell membranes, enabling endosome-independent cytoplasmic delivery of the genetic payloads. In orthotopic GBM models, Plofsome-mediated delivery of siMDK or Cas9 RNP targeting MDK effectively silenced or edited the MDK gene, disrupted the MDK-CD109-STAT3 signaling pathway, and re-sensitized tumors to TMZ, resulting in tumor growth inhibition and prolonged survival. Importantly, the system was selectively activated within ROS-rich tumor regions, remaining inert in healthy brain tissue, thus ensuring high therapeutic precision and safety [91].

Likewise, Rouatbi et al. (2024) developed a non-viral lipid nanoparticle (LNP) platform for in vivo CRISPR–Cas9 gene editing in GSCs. The LNPs co-encapsulated Cas9 messenger RNA (mCas9) and a single-guide RNA (sgRNA) targeting a model gene, green fluorescent protein (GFP). In vitro studies demonstrated effective protection of the RNA cargo from serum-mediated degradation. Following a single intratumoral injection in orthotopic GSC tumor models, the LNPs mediated gene-editing efficiencies of approximately 80% within SOX2⁺ GSC populations by day 14, accompanied by an approximately twofold reduction in GFP protein expression. Notably, the LNP platform significantly outperformed a Lipofectamine™ Stem in vitro [92]. Following this work, Rouatbi et al. (2025) demonstrated an advance by employing CRISPR-RNA-LNP to achieve precise immune-checkpoint editing and immune reprogramming in the highly resistant mesenchymal GBM subtype by targeting two immune-checkpoints. The CRISPR–LNPs were composed of ionizable lipid DLin-MC3-DMA, DSPC, cholesterol, and DMG-PEG 2000, for endosome escape while maintaining high serum stability. The CRISPR–LNPs encapsulated Cas9 mRNA and sgRNAs targeting both PD-L1 and CD47 (Fig. 4A). Employing NPE-IE cells that closely mirror human GBM pathology this formulation achieved ~ 69–77% indel production (Fig. 4B-C) and resulted in the efficient protein knock-out of CD47. Following intracranial administration, there was significant uptake of the LNPs within both tumor cells and tumor-associated macrophages, allowing for the concurrent modulation of malignant and immune compartments respectively. In addition, these LNPs mediated PD-L1 and CD47 editing in orthotopic tumor. Although PD-L1 knock-out alone was found to have limited benefits, CD47 knock-out induced a large anti-tumor effect in that it delayed tumor progression with significant enhancement of treatment outcome, leading to decreased tumor burden (Fig. 4E-F) and enhanced infiltration of tumor-associated macrophages and in particular CD8⁺ cytotoxic T lymphocytes (Fig. 4D) [93]. This work demonstrated that immune-checkpoint LNPs can integrate immune modulation and genome correction within a single nanocarrier, achieving multi-layered reprogramming of mesenchymal GBM through rational lipid design and coordinated barrier adaptation.

Together, these studies illustrate the rapid evolution of barrier-adaptive genome-editing LNPs capable of integrating vascular navigation, cellular uptake, endosomal escape, and immune modulation within a unified nanoplatform. By combining rational lipid chemistry with precise genetic targeting, these systems demonstrate the potential to couple genome editing with tumor microenvironment remodeling in glioblastoma models. While still at a preclinical stage, such CRISPR–LNP platforms highlight a promising direction toward multifunctional, genetically precise therapeutic strategies.

Despite this therapeutic promise, important safety considerations remain. Off-target genome editing, unintended indel formation, and the potential for long-term genomic instability represent key translational challenges that require rigorous evaluation in clinically relevant models. In addition, immune responses to Cas proteins and prolonged nuclease expression may influence safety profiles, particularly in the context of repeated administration. Continued optimization of guide RNA specificity, strategies to ensure transient nuclease expression, and comprehensive genome-wide off-target analyses will be essential for clinical translation to maximize therapeutic precision while minimizing unintended genomic perturbation. sec.title: Biomimetic nanoparticles for nucleic-acid delivery for treating glioblastoma
sec.p: Whereas Sect. ''LNPs in Glioblastoma Therapy'' focuses primarily on recent advances in synthetic lipid systems optimized for barrier navigation and intracellular release and their applications, Sect. ''Biomimetic Nanoparticles for Nucleic-Acid Delivery for Treating Glioblastom'' shifts attention to biomimetic nanocarriers, which is a rapidly advancing class of delivery systems that integrate natural biological interfaces or closely engineered structural mimics. Unlike conventional ionizable LNPs that often depend on exogenous targeting ligands, biomimetic architectures harness native membrane proteins and lipid compositions to mediate physiologically relevant interactions. These include receptor-mediated transcytosis across the BBB, immune evasion through the presentation of self-markers, and homotypic recognition enabling glioblastoma-specific targeting [94]. Recent advances have underscored the therapeutic potential of these biologically inspired platforms, encompassing cell-membrane–coated nanoparticles, lipoprotein-mimicking systems, virus- and bacteriophage-like nanocarriers, DNA-based nanostructures, and engineered or exosome-inspired extracellular vesicles. These approaches represent the next generation of intelligent, adaptive nanomedicines designed to replicate nature’s transport and communication mechanisms for efficient and precise nucleic-acid delivery in glioblastoma.

sec.title: Cell membrane coated nanoparticles
sec.p: Membrane coated biomimetic nanoparticles are defined as nanoparticles coated with biological membranes or their engineered hybrids which preserve native membrane proteins and lipids which allow immune evasion, receptor-mediated transcytosis, and homotypic targeting of tumors. These membrane types include those derived from red blood cells, platelets, macrophages, stem cells, and tumor cells, as well as hybrids which combine a plurality of sources to integrate biologically complementary functions these systems inherit biological functions, including immune evasion, receptor-mediated transcytosis, and homotypic targeting permitting their circumvention from systemic clearance effector systems and their high biocompatibility in traversing the BBB. While earlier reviews have largely had their focus on biomimetic strategies for utilizing properties for enhanced chemotherapy efficacy [94], the present section highlights recent advances in membrane-coated biomimetic nanoparticles engineered for nucleic-acid delivery to remodel the glioblastoma tumor microenvironment. Building prior immune-stealth and barrier-crossing platforms, emerging designs now integrate gene regulation with redox, hypoxia, ferroptotic, metabolic remodeling, and inducing apoptosis, enabling active reprogramming of the GBM microenvironment.

sec.title: Cell membrane coated nanoparticles for redox-mediated remodeling via RNAi and chemodynamic synergy
sec.p: GBM maintains survival in part through strong antioxidant buffering and anti-apoptotic signaling; redox-targeted biomimetic systems aim to collapse this defense and force oxidative lethality while delivering RNAi. For instance, Zhang et al. (2022) reported a redox-responsive nanoplatform (MPC@siBcl-2) combining chemodynamic therapy (CDT) with small interfering RNA (siRNA)-mediated gene silencing to remodel oxidative stress and enhance apoptosis in GBM. The nanoparticle exhibited a core–shell structure consisting of: (i) a metastatic melanoma cell membrane coating to facilitate homotypic targeting and blood–brain barrier (BBB) interaction; (ii) a pH-responsive poly-L-lysine–citraconic anhydride (PLL-CA) intermediate layer enabling charge reversal within endosomal/lysosomal compartments to promote endosomal escape and siRNA release; and (iii) a polyethyleneimine-xanthate (PEX) core complexed with B-cell lymphoma 2 (Bcl-2) siRNA. In the reductive tumor microenvironment, PEX chelated Cu²⁺ ions and promoted their reduction to Cu⁺, catalyzing Fenton-like reactions with hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂). This process generated hydroxyl radicals, depleted intracellular glutathione (GSH), and increased oxidative stress. Concurrent Bcl-2 silencing reduced anti-apoptotic signaling, thereby enhancing susceptibility to oxidative damage.The melanoma membrane cloak further enhanced BBB transcytosis through reversible ZO-1 downregulation and interactions with integrins and selectins, producing transient, non-damaging BBB opening (Fig. 5A-B). It was shown that, after 48 h incubation with NPs, the expression of ZO-1 was reduced but gradually recovered after 72 h incubation, confirming the NPs transiently opened the BBB for entering the brain (Fig. 5C-D). In vitro, MPC@siBcl-2 achieved efficient siRNA uptake, robust ROS generation, and potent Bcl-2 knockdown; in vivo, it prolonged circulation, enhanced brain accumulation. Notably, PBS- and free siBcl-2 treated mice showed rapid body-weight loss consistent with CNS dysfunction from unchecked GBM progression, whereas MPC@siBcl-2 markedly attenuated weight loss, in line with its superior tumor inhibition (Fig. 5E). Correspondingly, MPC@siBcl-2 extended median survival to 47 days, significantly longer than, the control, the MPC@siScr (Fig. 5F). Intratumoral copper quantification showed elevated Cu levels, and histological analyses showed less Ki-67 signaling and increased signals for caspase-3 and TUNEL, confirming extensive apoptosis (Fig. 5G) [95].

sec.title: Cell membrane coated nanoparticles for hypoxia remodeling and metabolic reprogramming
sec.p: Given the role of hypoxia in driving angiogenic signaling and therapy resistance in GBM, several recent studies have engineered microenvironment-responsive, biomimetic nanoplatforms by which to remodel hypoxic niches and potentiate energy-based therapies effective in the treatment of GBM. Li et al. (2022) introduced hypoxia-remodeling by implementing, cell membrane coated nanoparticles, ISZ@JUM, combined with sonodynamic therapy to remediate oxygen deprivation and potentiate ROS generation. ISZ@JUM possessed a macrophage-cancer hybrid-membrane nanoplatform, wherein zeolitic imidazolate framework-8 (ZIF-8) nanoparticles were co-loaded with indocyanine green (ICG), a sonosensitizer, and HIF-1α siRNA, which were then cloaked with fused macrophage and GBM-cell membranes. The hybrid coating endowed the nanoparticles with both BBB penetrability and capability to home to the tumor. Once ISZ@JUM internalized within tumor tissue, the acidic microenvironment triggered ZIF-8 degradation, effecting the release of ICG and HIF-1α siRNA. The silencing of HIF-1α remediated hypoxia, and amplified ROS generation while allowing for synergistic SDT efficacy. In vitro and in vivo analyses confirmed BBB penetrability, increased GBM accumulation, and SDT–RNAi synergy with negligible systemic toxicity [96]. Similarly, Wang et al. (2023) advanced the same concept yet a step further by developing a biomimetic, hypoxia-triggered RNAi nanomedicine, poly(MIs)/PTX@PEI/siPGK1@CCM, which synergistically amplified outcomes from chemotherapy and radiotherapy through metabolic reprogramming. Their system combined a hypoxia-sensitive amphiphilic polymer for triggered release of both paclitaxel and siRNA against PGK1, with a cancer-cell-membrane cloak for immune evasion and BBB transcytosis. By effecting PGK1 silencing, a glycolytic enzyme that promotes energy metabolism and radioresistance, the formulation effectively disrupted tumor bioenergetics, resensitizing GBM cells to radiation and amplifying DNA damage induced by paclitaxel. In orthotopic GBM models, the nanoparticles achieved high BBB penetrability, selective tumor accumulation, and a promising median survival of 77.5 days, without manifest systemic toxicity [97].

In addition to RNAi, Chen et al. (2024) developed a hybrid membrane–camouflaged nanosensitizer, CNL@miPA, which integrates miR therapy and radiotherapy to target hypoxia-driven GBM. Realizing that tumor hypoxia and PLK1 overexpression drive radioresistance and malignant conversion, the authors designed NPs that co-deliver gold nanoclusters and miR-593–5p. The system’s core tackles the tumor’s defenses on two fronts. First, to reverse the radio-protective hypoxia, the gold nanocluster core acts as a built-in oxygen generator, catalyzing the decomposition of tumor-abundant hydrogen peroxide. It also functions as an intrinsic radiosensitizer. Second, to disrupt the cancer cells’ molecular machinery, the nanoparticle delivers miR-593–5p, a tumor-suppressor microRNA that silences the PLK1 oncogene. This targeted delivery is enabled by a biomimetic cloak of cancer and NK cell membranes, which facilitates BBB crossing and tumor homing. When localized to the hypoxic tumor site, the system generated oxygen and ROS, effectively alleviating hypoxia and amplifying radiotherapy-induced oxidative stress. Concomitantly, silencing of PLK1 by miR-593–5p enhanced apoptosis and sensitized GBM cells to radiation. In orthotopic GBM models, the developed NPs exhibited prolonged systemic circulation, significant tumor accumulation, and potent synergistic tumor suppression when combined with radiotherapy, greatly prolonging survival without systemic toxicity [98]. In summary, these studies illuminate how microenvironment-responsive, membrane-coated RNAi and miRNA nanoplatforms may be exploited to reoxygenate hypoxic GBM tissue, reprogram tumor metabolism, and potentiate energy-based therapies, establishing an integrated framework for hypoxia-remodeling nanomedicine in glioblastoma.

sec.title: Cell membrane coated nanoparticles for apoptosis-drive therapy
sec.p: Apoptosis is a tightly regulated form of programmed cell death that maintains tissue homeostasis but is frequently impaired in glioblastoma, contributing to tumor persistence and therapy resistance. Restoring apoptotic signaling through nucleic-acid delivery has therefore become an essential therapeutic goal, and recent advances in cell-membrane-coated nanoparticles have provided an efficient means to deliver such genetic payloads across the BBB while minimizing immune clearance.

To overcome the poor stability and limited brain delivery of mRNA therapeutics, Liu et al. (2023) developed a multifunctional, erythrocyte-membrane-camouflaged biomimetic nanoparticle (ABNPs@mRNA) for targeted mRNA transport into GBM. The red-blood-cell-membrane (RBCm) coating serves as a natural stealthy layer that minimizes immunogenicity and prolongs systemic circulation. For brain-specific targeting, ApoE peptides were conjugated to the RBCm surface, enabling LDLR-mediated transcytosis across the BBB and preferential uptake by GBM cells. To achieve efficient intracellular cargo release, a charge-conversional polymer core was engineered to respond to the mildly acidic endosomal environment, destabilizing the RBCm shell and accelerating endosomal escape. These design elements yielded ABNPs@mRNA, which encapsulates phosphatase and tensin homolog deleted on chromosome 10 (PTEN) mRNA, a tumor-suppressor transcript commonly deleted or mutated in 20–40% of GBM cases. Restoration of PTEN expression re-establishes the negative regulation of the PI3K–AKT–mTOR pathway, thereby suppressing tumor proliferation, angiogenesis, and survival, while promoting apoptotic and necroptotic cell death. In PTEN-deficient GBM models, ABNPs@mRNA restored PTEN protein levels comparable to those achieved using commercial Lipofectamine 2k. In orthotopic GBM mouse models, systemic administration of ABNPs@mRNA inhibited tumor growth, prolonged median survival, and produced negligible off-target toxicity [99].

sec.title: Cell membrane coated nanoparticles for ferroptosis-driven immunotherapy
sec.p: Ferroptosis, an iron-dependent form of lipid-peroxidation, is being exploited for elimination of therapy-resistant GBM, and next-generation membrane-coated nanoparticles are now being devised that couple ferroptotic stress to develop a ferroptosis-driven immunotherapeutic nanoplatform to address the poor immunogenicity and resistance of GBM. For instance, Liu et al. (2023) designed a biomimetic ferroptosis-inducing nanoplatform that combines ferroptosis induction with immune checkpoint blockade. The system integrates Fe₃O₄ magnetic nanoparticles loaded with siPD-L1 and cloaked with BV2 microglial cell membranes, which confer BBB penetration, tumor-homing capability, and immune compatibility. Upon reaching the tumor, Fe²⁺ ions released from Fe₃O₄ catalyzed lipid peroxidation, generating reactive oxygen species and triggering ferroptotic cell death, while siPD-L1 silencing alleviated tumor-induced immune suppression. In orthotopic drug-resistant GBM animal models, Fe₃O₄-siPD-L1@M-BV2 demonstrated high tumor accumulation of both siPD-L1 and Fe²⁺, which effectively downregulated PD-L1 and elicited robust ferroptosis. The ensuing ferroptosis stress promoted dendritic-cell maturation and reprogrammed the tumor immune microenvironment to an antitumor phenotype as indicated by an increased CD8⁺ T-cell-to-Treg ratio and M1-type microglial polarization. This bidirectional feedback loop, whereby ferroptosis increases immune activation and immune activation enhances ferroptosis, resulted in a cascade amplification effect that produced strong tumor suppression and prolonged survival in vivo [100]. In another study, Cao et al. (2023), instead of employing magnetic nanoparticles as ferroptosis inducers, identified arachidonate 15-lipoxygenase (ALOX15) as a key ferroptosis driver through CRISPR–Cas9 screening and subsequently designed a small-activating RNA (saALOX15)-based cell membrane coated NPs to therapeutically activate this pathway. SaRNAs, unlike siRNA or miRNA that produce post-transcriptional gene-silencing effects by promoting degradation of mRNA or blocking translation, bind to the promoter-associated regions of target genes, causing their transcription to be activated. The saALOX15 payload was encapsulated within mesoporous polydopamine nanoparticles and cloaked with Angiopep-2–modified macrophage membranes, forming Ang-MMsaNPs. The Angiopep-2 ligand facilitated LRP1-mediated transcytosis across the BBB, while macrophage-derived CD47 and integrins minimized mononuclear-phagocyte-system clearance, thereby prolonging systemic circulation. Ang-MMsaNPs exhibited a uniform core–shell morphology and excellent storage stability. Following systemic administration, the nanoparticles efficiently escaped endosomes and released saALOX15 into the cytoplasm, where it transcriptionally upregulated ALOX15 expression, induced extensive lipid peroxidation and mitochondrial injury, and significantly reduced tumor volume as a single treatment. Importantly, Ang-MMsaNPs exhibited synergistic effects with radiotherapy (RT) in the orthotopic GBM mouse model. Bioluminescence imaging showed that tumor growth was suppressed in all treatment groups compared to the PBS, while Ang-MMsaNPs alone induced reduction in TSZ-LN229 tumor growth. Ang-MMsaNPs with radiotherapy resulted in significantly smaller tumor volumes, delayed progression and prolonged survival compared to either treatment alone. Mechanistically, Ang-MMsaNP treatment upregulated the expression of ALOX15, which was further enhanced by RT. The immune-histochemical analysis of ACSL4 and 4-HNE, two crucial biomarkers of ferroptosis, and the increase in the level of malondialdehyde, confirmed increased ferroptosis in GBM cells. The highest induction was observed in the combination treatment group. These findings suggest that Ang-MMsaNPs enhance RT-induced ferroptosis and are associated with improved therapeutic outcomes in orthotopic GBM models [101].

Collectively, these studies indicate that the delivery of nucleic acids using membrane-coated biomimetic nanoparticles has transformed into an adaptive therapeutic system capable of microenvironmental reprogramming. The nanoplatforms that have integrated gene regulation with redox, hypoxia, ferroptotic remodeling, thus convert the metabolic and oxidative vulnerabilities of GBM into therapeutic opportunities, bringing about a paradigm shift toward functionally intelligent biomimetic nanomedicines.
