sec.title: lipoprotein-, virus-, and DNA-mimicking nanoparticles
sec.p: With the use of cell-membrane coatings, biomimetic nanomedicine has increasingly embraced molecular and structural mimicry for nucleic acid delivery. Lipoprotein-mimicking nanoparticles mimic various structural and functional aspects of the endogenous high-density (HDL) and low-density lipoproteins (LDL) and thus taking advantage of receptor-mediated delivery pathways including LDLR and SR-BI to facilitate BBB transcytosis and tumor-specific accumulation. Despite these advantages, full analysis of the literature reveals that relatively few studies have been published, even over the last three years, utilizing lipoprotein-mimicking systems for nucleic acid delivery to GBM. HDL-mimicking nanoparticles, however, have been considerably advanced as agents for use in the treatment of atherosclerosis, primarily directed at increasing cholesterol efflux and plaque regression rather than co-delivery of gene treatments or brain-targeting applications. A recent example is the tumor-penetrating HDL-mimetic nanoparticle developed by Wang et al. (2022), which integrates photo-gene therapy to overcome glioma hypoxia and therapeutic resistance, a strategy conceptually aligned with the cell-membrane-coated nanoplatforms discussed in Sect. ''Cell membrane coated nanoparticles''. The nanoplatform was engineered by fusing the tumor-penetrating peptide tLyP-1 to an ApoA-I-mimicking D4F peptide, forming an HDL-like carrier capable of crossing the BBB and BBTB via NRP-1-mediated transcytosis. It co-delivered ICG as a near-infrared (NIR) photosensitizer and photothermal agent and cholesterol-conjugated HIF-1α siRNA anchored on the lipid monolayer. Upon IR light administration, therefore, ICG produced ROS and local hyperthermia, causing collapse of the nanostructure and release of the siRNA on demand. This photo-induced gene silencing downregulated HIF-1α and VEGF, alleviating hypoxia and suppressing angiogenesis. When used in orthotopic GBM models, ptHDL/siHIF-ICG achieved enhanced BBB transcytosis, deep tumor penetration, and tumor-specific accumulation. Combined NIR-triggered phototherapy and RNAi induced apoptosis, inhibited tumor growth, and extended survival without systemic toxicity [102]. Moving beyond photo-gene therapy, Yang et al. (2023) demonstrated the immunotherapeutic potential of HDL-mimicking nanocarriers for RNA delivery. They engineered a synthetic HDL (sHDL)-based nanomedicine that co-delivered three key payloads: siRNA against SOCS1 (siSOCS1), an immunostimulatory peptide adjuvant, and a BBB-penetrating peptide. This multifunctional platform leveraged SR-BI receptor-mediated transport to achieve targeted accumulation in the brain tumor. Within the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment, siSOCS1 silenced a critical immune checkpoint, which in turn reprogrammed the immune landscape. This was evidenced by dendritic cell maturation, a surge in tumor-infiltrating cytotoxic CD8⁺ T-cells, and a simultaneous reduction in regulatory T-cells and M2 macrophages. The concerted action of these effects triggered an antitumor immune response, resulting in tumor regression without observable systemic toxicity in orthotopic GBM models [103].

In addition to lipid-mimicking nanoparticles, Zhu et al. (2024) developed virus-mimicking nanoparticles (VMNs) by regulating protein conformation through lipid nanoenvironments, enabling precise cell-selective RNA delivery in glioblastoma. These VMNs efficiently crossed the BBB, escaped lysosomal degradation, and achieved targeted siRNA delivery in orthotopic GBM models, resulting in tumor suppression and prolonged survival [104]. Building on this concept, Pang et al. (2023) designed bioengineered hybrids that combine bacteriophage and viral-like properties to exploit natural genetic-delivery mechanisms. Specifically, they engineered Qβ bacteriophage–derived virus-like particles as programmable RNAi nanocarriers by incorporating a fluorescent broccoli-tagged three-way junction RNA scaffold capable of co-loading EGFR siRNA and let-7 g microRNA within a single self-assembling capsid. The resulting construct, TrQβ@b-3WJLet-7gsiEGFR, was further modified with a TAT peptide to enhance cellular uptake and delivered via convection-enhanced intracranial infusion, effectively bypassing the BBB and promoting endosomal escape. Within tumor tissue, this dual-RNA scaffold simultaneously silenced EGFR and NF-κB–associated DNA-repair pathways, sensitizing glioblastoma cells to radiotherapy. In orthotopic GBM models, the treatment suppressed tumor proliferation and invasion and, importantly, synergized with radiotherapy to extend survival without systemic toxicity [105].

Beyond lipid and viral mimicry, DNA-based biomimetic nanostructures bring structural precision and programmability to nucleic-acid delivery. Song et al. (2024) constructed tetrahedral DNA nanocages (tFNAs) and cloaked within a folate-modified erythrocyte–cancer-cell–macrophage hybrid membrane for treating GBM. Tetrahedral DNA nanostructures are those that allow the assembly of components in a precisely programmable manner, while they show excellent biocompatibility properties and versatile load-carrying systems used [106]. The coating thus provided prolonged circulation properties, immune evasion characteristics and the tumor targeting by folate-receptor-mediated means. In orthotopic GBM models, the nanocages demonstrated increased tumor accumulation and were associated with prolonged survival [107]. Lan et al. (2024) reported a DNA nanoframework–based delivery system designed for gene silencing with structural programmability. The platform consisted of a six-helix DNA bundle engineered to encapsulate siRNA targeting O⁶-methylguanine-DNA methyltransferase (siMGMT). A dual nucleolin-responsive locking mechanism was incorporated to shield the siRNA cargo during circulation and enable release within tumor tissue. The construct was further modified with Angiopep-2 peptides to facilitate BBB transcytosis. In orthotopic glioblastoma models, this Angiopep-2-FNN-siMGMT achieved efficient BBB penetration, selective MGMT knock-down, and induced a reduction in the IC50 of TMZ, resulting in a 2-fold longer survival extension compared with TMZ alone. Importantly, no systemic or hematologic toxicity was observed, highlighting the biocompatibility of DNA-framework carriers [108].

sec.title: Exosome-based and exosome-inspired delivery systems
sec.p: Exosomes are a specific subclass of extracellular vesicles of endosomal origin, distinguished by their unique lipid–protein composition. Enriched in tetraspanins, adhesion molecules, and membrane fusion proteins, they are nature’s optimized nanocarriers for intercellular communication [109]. These inherent biological properties enable exosomes to overcome key therapeutic barriers: they evade immune clearance through surface markers, cross the BBB via receptor-mediated transcytosis, and home to tumor sites through chemokine-guided tropism. Their endogenous origin ensures superior biocompatibility and robust stability [110]. These combined traits make exosomes, and their engineered derivatives, uniquely powerful platforms for nucleic acid delivery in GBM.

sec.title: Engineered exosome and exosome-inspired systems
sec.p: Recent advances in engineered exosomes have led to a transformation of their natural intercellular messenger role into sophisticated hybrid systems for specific nucleic acid delivery for GBM. While previous reviews have outlined the therapeutic aspect to exosomes in glioblastoma prior to 2022 in response to small drug [111–113], this section focuses on examining contemporary advances in engineered exosome systems and exosome inspired systems for nucleic acid delivery for GBM.

For instance, Qian et al. (2022) demonstrated that engineered neural stem cell-derived exosomes loaded with miR-124-3p effectively inhibited glioma cell proliferation and migration by suppressing oncogenic targets such as FLOT2 and ADAM15, underscoring the capacity of exosomal miRNA transfer to reprogram tumor cells [112]. Another interesting study also generated exosomes with miR-124 function in a dual-gene manner. Yueh et al. (2025) engineered umbilical-cord derived mesenchymal stem cells (UMSCs) which co-expressed both miR-124 and PD-1 to create a dual-gene cellular delivery system and associated therapeutic exosomes for GBM. These engineered UMSCs maintained their stemness ability and actively targeted the intracranial glioblastoma location and released exosomes enriched in the payload of miR-124. Subsequently, both engineered UMSCs and their secreted exosomes were able to inhibit GBM cell proliferation and able to induce apoptosis. The systemic delivery of the dual-gene engineered UMSCs or their exosomes was able to markedly reduce the tumor burden in orthotopic GBM models from which the activation of immune cells significantly improved [114].

In another study, Liu et al. (2023) reported An2–functionalized engineered STAT3-siRNA-loaded exosomes (Exo-An2-siRNA) capable of efficiently crossing the BBB and silencing STAT3 in orthotopic U87MG models. The An2 modification enhanced BBB penetration and glioma targeting, leading to significant tumor growth inhibition and prolonged median survival in mice [115]. In addition, McDonald et al. (2024) developed a novel engineered-exosome (eExo) system derived from HEK293T cells and contained a polycistronic plasmid (pPolymiR) coding for three anti-glioma miRNAs, miR-124-2, miR-135a-2 and let-7i. In the engineered eExos, viral proteins Gag and RB19g were incorporated to enhance the packaging of the plasmid, cellular uptake and escape from lysosomes. In vitro studies showed that the use of eExos+pPolymiR induced significant inhibition of glioma stem cell viability with a selective modulation of gene expression in a synergistic manner. In vivo study showed that a single intracranial delivery led to a marked inhibition of the progression of the tumor with a significant increase in survival compared to treatment with miRNA alone [116]. The study highlights the potential of eExos as a versatile platform for delivering multiplexed RNA therapeutics to GBM. Later, Lu et al. (2025) developed a more sophisticated extracellular ferritin-armed vesicle (EV) platform of which M1 microglia derived exosomes were coated with H-ferritin (HFn) and co-loaded with siRNA targeting monocarboxylate transporter 4 (siMCT4) and ultrasmall Au/MnO₂ nanoparticles. This multifunctional nanoplatform was designed for the simultaneous disruption of tumor metabolic function and relief of microenvironmental immunosuppression. The combination of HFn with the exosome membranes gave these modified hybrid vesicles dual-targeting abilities, the innate tumor homing property of the M1 exosomes and transferrin-receptor binding properties of HFn permitting enhanced blood-brain barrier penetrability and glioma homing. Mechanistically, siMCT4 inhibition led to a lowering of lactate efflux allowing for intra-cellular buildup of lactate that induced tumor cell apoptosis from excess lactate and could in turn reprogram the TAMs from a pro-tumor M2 phenotype into an anti-tumor M1 phenotype. The Au/MnO₂ nanoparticles exerted a synergistic therapeutic effect: Au nanoparticles depleted glucose to induce starvation therapy, while MnO₂ catalyzed the conversion of endogenous metabolic byproducts into cytotoxic hydroxyl radicals via chemodynamic reactions, promoting oxidative stress and leading to increased death for the tumor cells [117].

Despite the progress in engineered exosomes, the loading of nucleic acid in exosomes is low. Thus, Lee et al. (2025) introduced an exosome–polymer hybrid nanocomplex designed to achieve systemic plasmid DNA (pDNA) delivery across the BBB. The engineered hybrid platform was created by complexing pDNA with a polyamidoamine dendrimer for higher loading efficiency, then coating it with exosome membranes and decorating the surface with T7 peptide, a transferring-receptor ligand that enhances BBB transcytosis. The T7-functionalized hybrids also achieved superior transfection efficiency and cytocompatibility compared with polymer- or EM-free counterparts by entering cells via clathrin- and caveolae-mediated endocytosis followed by proton-sponge–driven endosomal escape [118].

In addition, Zhang et al. (2025) created a promising exosome-inspired RNA-delivery nanoplatform that merges natural exosomal regulatory mechanisms with synthetic LNP engineering, marking a pivotal step toward multifunctional, barrier-adaptive therapeutics. The team identified circPRKD3, a circular RNA downregulated in glioma-stem-cell–derived exosomes (GDEs), where its loss results in poor patient prognosis. Mechanistically, GDE-circPRKD3 binds to the RNA-binding protein HNRNPC, which competitively inhibits HNRNPC from stabilizing IL6ST mRNA, leading to its decay and subsequent suppression of the oncogenic STAT3 signaling pathway. To restore this pathway’s regulation in vivo, the group constructed LNP-circPRKD3, a brain-targeted lipid LNP system modified with angiopep-2 for BBB transcytosis and cytosolic RNA release. Systemic administration of LNP-circPRKD3 efficaciously delivered circPRKD3, silenced STAT3 signaling, reprogrammed the GBM immune microenvironment switch TAMs from M2-like to an M1-like phenotype. This resulted in enhanced CXCL10 secretion, CD8⁺ T-infiltration and cytotoxicity. When combined with anti-PD-1 immune checkpoint blockade, the treatment achieved synergistic tumor growth inhibition and a significant survival benefit with negligible systemic toxicity [119]. Together, these findings position the integration of exosome-derived regulatory circRNAs with translational LNP architecture as a next-generation strategy to unite molecular precision, immune reprogramming, and manufacturable nanomedicine for durable GBM control.

sec.title: Evolution of lipid nanoparticle platforms for nucleic acid therapeutics
sec.p: Over the past decade, particularly within the last several years, LNP systems have undergone a remarkable evolution from simple RNA silencing carriers into highly engineered nanotherapeutic platforms capable of precise and multimodal modulation of glioblastoma biology. Advances in ionizable lipid chemistry and formulation engineering have enabled efficient encapsulation, protection, and cytosolic delivery of diverse nucleic acid cargos, including siRNA, mRNA, circRNA, plasmid DNA, and CRISPR–Cas genome-editing systems. Optimization of ionizable lipid pKa, membrane fusion properties, and lipid composition has substantially improved endosomal escape efficiency, historically one of the principal intracellular barriers to nucleic acid delivery. These advances have transformed LNP systems into multifunctional therapeutic platforms capable of modulating tumor resistance pathways, reshaping immunosuppressive tumor microenvironments, and enabling durable genetic intervention.

sec.title: Clinical translation and manufacturing maturity of LNP systems
sec.p: The clinical validation of RNA–LNP therapeutics reflects the convergence of molecular design and industrial scalability [120–122]. RNA drug substance manufacturing is enabled by modular in vitro transcription platforms compatible with nucleotide modification strategies that enhance stability and attenuate innate immune activation [123, 124]. Downstream purification workflows—integrating enzymatic digestion, chromatographic separation, and tangential flow filtration—ensure removal of residual DNA, double-stranded RNA contaminants, truncated transcripts, and reaction byproducts, thereby aligning product purity with regulatory expectations [125, 126].

Nanoparticle encapsulation via controlled microfluidic mixing provides reproducible self-assembly under tightly parameterized physicochemical conditions [127, 128]. Precise control over lipid ratios, RNA-to-lipid charge balance, solvent composition, and flow dynamics enables scalable production with consistent particle size, encapsulation efficiency, and structural integrity [127–129]. Critically, LNP systems possess well-defined critical quality attributes, including particle size distribution, polydispersity index, lipid composition, RNA integrity, sterility, and endotoxin levels, which can be quantitatively monitored and validated under GMP. This combination of chemically defined architecture, process control, and regulatory precedent positions LNPs among the most clinically advanced non-viral nucleic acid delivery platforms currently available.

sec.title: Biomimetic platforms: biological advantages and translational challenges
sec.p: Biomimetic nanoparticle platforms, including membrane-coated systems, lipoprotein-mimetic carriers, and extracellular vesicle–derived formulations, offer biologically inspired mechanisms of cellular interaction, leveraging endogenous membrane proteins and glycans to facilitate receptor-mediated uptake and immune modulation. In principle, such systems may recapitulate physiological trafficking pathways and attenuate immune recognition.

However, their translational trajectory remains constrained by inherent biological variability. Donor-dependent membrane composition, heterogeneity in glycoprotein distribution, and variability in isolation methodologies introduce batch-to-batch inconsistency that complicates definition and control of critical quality attributes. Moreover, nucleic acid cargo loading relies on post-isolation techniques, such as electroporation, sonication, or passive incubation—that frequently exhibit lower encapsulation efficiency and reduced reproducibility relative to electrostatic self-assembly in LNP systems. These methods can perturb membrane integrity, alter protein orientation, and destabilize vesicle structure, thereby limiting dose precision and complicating GMP adaptation. Consequently, although biomimetic platforms offer compelling biological functionality, their mechanistic predictability and regulatory readiness remain less advanced than those of chemically defined LNP architectures (Table 3).

sec.title: Cargo diversity and formulation requirements for lipid nanoparticles
sec.p: LNP functions according to a mechanistically unified design framework grounded in membrane biophysics and intracellular trafficking principles. Central to this framework is the incorporation of ionizable lipids engineered with an apparent pKa typically within the range of ~ 6.2–6.6, enabling particles to remain largely neutral under physiological conditions while acquiring positive charge within acidifying endosomal compartments. Conditional protonation promotes electrostatic interaction with anionic endosomal phospholipids and facilitates transient non-bilayer phase formation, destabilizing the endosomal membrane and enabling cytosolic release of nucleic acid cargo. Because endosomal escape represents the principal intracellular bottleneck in non-viral gene delivery, synchronization of lipid protonation kinetics with endosomal maturation is a primary determinant of in vivo potency. This escape mechanism is embedded within a structurally defined four-component architecture, ionizable lipid, helper phospholipid, cholesterol, and PEG-lipid, assembled reproducibly via controlled microfluidic mixing to achieve high encapsulation efficiency and scalable manufacturing consistency [136, 137].

Within this conserved mechanistic framework, optimal nanoparticle formulation is strongly influenced by the physicochemical and biological properties of the therapeutic payload. Distinct nucleic acid modalities, including siRNA, mRNA, circRNA, plasmid DNA (pDNA), and CRISPR–Cas systems, differ in molecular size, topology, charge density, intracellular localization requirements, and duration of activity. These differences impose cargo-specific constraints on encapsulation stability, nanoparticle size, lipid composition, intracellular trafficking behavior, and release kinetics. Short, rigid siRNA duplexes (~ 21–23 nucleotides) require rapid cytosolic availability to engage the RNA-induced silencing complex, making efficient early endosomal escape the dominant design priority. Formulations therefore emphasize tightly tuned ionizable lipid pKa, high escape probability, and particle diameters commonly in the 50–80 nm range to facilitate cellular uptake. In contrast, mRNA cargos, often 1–10 kb in length and conformationally flexible, require enhanced structural stabilization and sustained cytosolic persistence to support translation. These properties typically favor slightly larger particles, robust encapsulation efficiency, and carefully balanced lipid composition to minimize RNA degradation while maintaining escape competence. CircRNA, although inherently more nuclease-resistant, introduces additional requirements for prolonged intracellular retention and controlled release kinetics, often motivating increased structural stabilization within the particle core. Larger cargos, including pDNA and CRISPR–Cas ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complexes, impose further architectural constraints. Their increased size and charge density influence encapsulation efficiency and may necessitate moderately increased ionizable lipid content to maintain electrostatic stability. For pDNA and RNP systems, intracellular trafficking beyond cytosolic release, including nuclear access, becomes an additional rate-limiting consideration, shifting formulation priorities toward intracellular persistence and structural protection rather than exclusively rapid escape. In CRISPR mRNA systems, efficient but transient protein expression is desired, requiring rapid cytosolic release coupled with controlled stability.

sec.title: Delivery route considerations
sec.p: Delivery route selection represents a critical determinant of translational success. While intravenous administration remains the predominant clinical approach, alternative delivery strategies, including intrathecal, intracerebroventricular, intranasal, and convection-enhanced delivery, can partially or completely bypass blood–brain barrier transport constraints. These approaches enable direct nanoparticle exposure to central nervous system tissues and may substantially enhance delivery efficiency when intrinsic BBB permeability is limited. Optimal route selection must be integrated with nanoparticle physicochemical design, as particle size, surface chemistry, biodegradability, and cargo properties collectively influence CNS distribution, cellular uptake, safety, and therapeutic efficacy.

sec.title: Advanced preclinical model development
sec.p: Despite substantial technological progress, efficient and reproducible nanoparticle delivery to human brain tumors remains a major translational challenge. Ligand-mediated targeting strategies have demonstrated promising preclinical performance but often exhibit reduced efficiency in human-relevant systems due to species-specific receptor biology, receptor saturation, intracellular trafficking constraints, and heterogeneous receptor expression across tumor regions and patient populations. Thus, continued development of physiologically relevant human-based models, including BBB-on-chip systems, vascularized tissue constructs, and patient-derived organoids, will be essential for improving predictive accuracy and accelerating clinical translation.

sec.title: Artificial intelligence and high-throughput screening
sec.p: Artificial intelligence and high-throughput screening technologies are transforming nanoparticle discovery and optimization. Machine learning–guided lipid design, automated formulation platforms, and large-scale screening approaches enable systematic interrogation of nanoparticle structure–function relationships at unprecedented scale. These tools facilitate identification of optimal ionizable lipid chemistry, prediction of biodistribution patterns, and rapid iterative refinement of nanoparticle formulations based on biological performance data. AI-driven optimization provides a powerful framework for accelerating nanoparticle development while improving delivery efficiency and translational predictability.

sec.title: Viral-inspired design principles
sec.p: Engineered viral vectors developed through in vivo capsid selection provide valuable mechanistic insights into efficient central nervous system delivery [142]. Highly diverse adeno-associated virus capsid libraries are subjected to physiological selection pressures in vivo, enriching for variants capable of navigating circulation, binding endothelial receptors, crossing the blood–brain barrier, and entering target CNS cells [143]. Integration of high-throughput sequencing and machine learning enables identification of delivery architectures optimized under physiologically relevant conditions. Biotechnology platforms developed by companies such as Dyno Therapeutics, Voyager Therapeutics, and Capsida Biotherapeutics have demonstrated the effectiveness of combining vivo selection with AI based computational optimization to develop CNS-targeted delivery systems [144, 145]. Although structurally distinct from synthetic nanoparticles, these biologically optimized capsids provide a functional blueprint for nanoparticle engineering. Incorporation of viral-inspired targeting principles, including optimized receptor engagement kinetics, trafficking pathways, and surface architecture, may enable development of next-generation virus mimicking nanoparticle systems with improved BBB penetration, enhanced CNS specificity, and superior translational performance.

sec.title: Integration with complementary delivery systems
sec.p: Integration with complementary delivery platforms represents another promising strategy for improving therapeutic performance. Controlled-release systems, including hydrogel-based delivery platforms, can enable sustained and localized release of nucleic acid therapeutics, improving spatial targeting, reducing systemic exposure, and enhancing therapeutic durability. Such hybrid delivery strategies may be particularly beneficial following surgical tumor resection, where localized nanoparticle retention may improve therapeutic efficacy and reduce tumor recurrence.
